text: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.

text: From the basin camp, the peak's south side shows two gullies separated by a dividing buttress, and picking the wrong one is the failure here. The right-hand gully is the trap: it cliffs out in a closed chimney and does not go. The line takes the minor rib on the climber's left of that rightmost gully. Get there by dropping about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek and making a rising traverse beneath the gully system, past the adjacent buttress. The proof higher up is the chockstones: the gully leading up to the Eye Col is blocked by large jammed blocks, and pitching past them, including one narrow crack normally taken on a belay, is the crux of reaching the notch. If the gully you are in runs clean with no chockstones and narrows into a closed chimney above, back off — that is the right-hand gully. Above the notch, easy slabs and scrambling lead to the summit.

text: Two trailheads serve this scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy.

text:
The trailhead is unmarked and the path start is a tree-line edge, so the find is at the road rather than on the mountain. The pullout is 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake Trailhead coming from Rainy Pass. If you have reached the Blue Lake Trailhead, you have driven 0.7 mile too far. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a stand of trees begins, and the boot path leaves from its west edge.

Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. A level section of ridge is the arrival, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit. The alternative, which is also correct: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

So the decision at 6,800 ft is a real fork and both branches work: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

The negative test against the other approach, which matters because both start within three miles of each other on the same highway: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a meadow basin at 6,100 ft below the west ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the south ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

text: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.

text: Windy Peak (8,335') is the easternmost of Washington's 100 highest peaks (the "Bulgers"), standing over the remote northeastern Pasayten Wilderness about 5 miles south of the Canadian border. Unlike most Bulgers, its standard route is a non-technical trail walk-up rather than a climb — it's cataloged here for peakbagging-list completeness, and the real challenge is logistical: a long, remote approach on gravel forest roads far from any town. A gabled-roof L-4 cab fire lookout was built on the summit in 1932 by E.W. Allen and Raymond Johnson, saw brief use in the WWII Aircraft Warning Service (Jul-Sep 1942), and was removed in 1963; remnants of its old telephone line are still visible on the northwest slope.

Stuart Lake trailhead to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path along the lake's west shore, Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft, then south across talus toward the tower and up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of it.

Published figures for the day put it at roughly six to eight hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point, which is a wide enough spread that it should be treated as a range rather than a plan.
